study.title: Dismantling the eDNA-mediated H<sub>2</sub>S barrier with biohybrids against refractory biofilm infections

cover.headline: Bacterial biofilms may use **hydrogen sulfide gas to jam immune defenses** and resist antibiotics

slides.title: This could point to new ways to treat persistent infections that antibiotics alone cannot clear.
slides.body:
The study found that biofilm bacteria create a defensive loop using hydrogen sulfide gas. This loop blocks immune cells and helps bacteria survive treatment.

The researchers built a system that breaks the loop and clears persistent bacteria in lab models.

slides.title: Extracellular DNA in biofilms is linked to local hydrogen sulfide enrichment, stronger barriers, and immune suppression.
slides.body:
The biofilm matrix traps and concentrates hydrogen sulfide from bacteria. This gas stabilizes the DNA scaffold and suppresses macrophage activity.

The engineered minicells target low-oxygen zones, scavenge hydrogen sulfide, and degrade the DNA matrix.

slides.title: Biofilm resilience is usually attributed to physical barriers and slow bacterial metabolism, not gas-mediated signaling.
slides.body:
Most research focuses on how biofilm structure blocks drug entry or how dormant bacteria evade antibiotics. Gas regulation has been less explored.

This work suggests that gaseous mediators like hydrogen sulfide actively maintain biofilm defenses in the local environment.

caveats: This study found a pattern, not a cause. Something else could explain the link between hydrogen sulfide and biofilm defense.
The biohybrid system was tested in lab models, not in human infections, so clinical effectiveness remains unknown.

source.abstract: The spatiotemporal distribution of gaseous mediators is critical for maintaining physiological functions. Biofilms both contain gas-producing bacteria and possess complex architectures that reshape gaseous mediator distribution. However, whether biofilm pathogenicity is linked to such gaseous regulation remains unclear. In this study, we reveal that extracellular DNA (eDNA) within the biofilm matrix contributes to the local retention and enrichment of H 2 S. This enrichment stabilizes eDNA, strengthens biofilm barriers, impedes gas clearance, promotes bacterial persistence, and induces macrophage immunosuppression, creating a reciprocally protective defensive loop. To dismantle this defense, we engineered a stepwise-responsive biohybrid system in which probiotic-derived engineered minicells actively target hypoxic biofilm regions, while H 2 S-triggered nanoparticle degradation enables deeper matrix penetration and concurrent H 2 S scavenging. The retained minicells then catalyze in situ glucose oxidation to generate H 2 O 2 , which, together with Fe 2+ -mediated Fenton-like reactions, degrades eDNA and collapses the biofilm. This strategy eradicates persistent bacteria, reverses immunosuppression, and provides a therapeutic strategy to reduce recurrence and optimize refractory infection treatments.
